question_text: A company needs to deploy a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Usage is highly variable — spiky during business hours, near-zero overnight. Which deployment option minimises cost while still meeting sub-3-second response SLA?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference via Lambda invocations
Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput with 24/7 reserved Model Units
A permanently running EC2 GPU instance
AWS Batch for FM inference jobs

explanation: Skill 2.2.1 lists Lambda for on-demand invocation as a deployment option for specific application needs. For variable, spiky workloads, on-demand Bedrock via Lambda is most cost-efficient — you pay per token, with no idle capacity cost. Provisioned Throughput commits to reserved capacity 24/7, cost-effective only for sustained high throughput. A permanent EC2 GPU instance has high idle cost. AWS Batch is for large batch jobs, not interactive FM inference.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock deployment options, Lambda, cost optimisation

question_text: A company is deploying a large open-source LLM (7B parameters) on Amazon SageMaker for production inference. Which deployment considerations are specific to LLMs compared to traditional ML models? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Container images must be optimised for multi-GPU memory requirements and efficient GPU utilisation
LLMs require specialised token-processing capacity planning, unlike traditional batch-prediction models
LLMs always require more CPU cores, not GPUs
LLMs use the same deployment artefacts as scikit-learn classifiers
LLMs can be deployed using standard single-instance SageMaker endpoints with no memory optimisation

explanation: Skill 2.2.2 describes container-based deployment patterns optimised for LLM memory requirements, GPU utilisation, and token processing capacity, plus specialised model loading strategies. LLMs require multi-GPU tensor parallelism, GPU memory management (KV cache), and token throughput capacity planning — all absent in traditional scikit-learn or XGBoost deployments. LLMs require GPUs, not just CPUs. Standard SageMaker instances lack the GPU memory optimisation LLMs need.
source_topic: LLM deployment, SageMaker, GPU, container optimisation

question_text: A company's GenAI application handles both simple FAQ queries and complex multi-step reasoning tasks. Using a large, expensive FM for all queries is too costly. Which strategy balances cost and quality?

options.text: Use only the smallest available model for all queries to minimise cost
Use API-based model cascading: route simple queries to a small, cheap FM; escalate to a larger FM only when complexity requires it
Fine-tune the large FM to be faster, then use it for everything
Cache all responses and serve cached answers to avoid FM calls

explanation: Skill 2.2.3 explicitly cites 'API-based model cascading to perform routine queries' and 'smaller pre-trained models for specific tasks' as optimised FM deployment approaches. A router that classifies query complexity and dispatches to the appropriate model tier (small for FAQ, large for complex reasoning) significantly reduces cost without degrading quality on hard queries. Using only small models sacrifices quality. Fine-tuning for speed is complex and expensive. Caching is useful but can't cover all unique queries.
source_topic: Model cascading, cost-efficient FM deployment

question_text: A company uses Amazon Bedrock for most inference but needs to run a proprietary fine-tuned model that cannot be hosted on Bedrock. Which architecture handles both?

options.text: Host the proprietary model on an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint; route requests to Bedrock or SageMaker based on model type
Deploy the proprietary model on Lambda with model weights bundled into the deployment package
Use Amazon Kendra to serve the proprietary model via an API
Upload the proprietary model to the Amazon Bedrock model catalogue for public use

explanation: Skill 2.2.1 cites SageMaker AI endpoints for hybrid solutions. A routing layer (e.g., Lambda + API Gateway) inspects the request and dispatches to Bedrock for hosted FMs and to a SageMaker real-time endpoint for the proprietary model. Lambda functions are size-constrained (< 10GB) — unsuitable for multi-gigabyte model weights. Amazon Kendra is a document search service. Models cannot be uploaded to Bedrock's public catalogue by arbitrary customers.
source_topic: SageMaker endpoints, Bedrock, hybrid deployment

question_text: A company runs a high-traffic FM inference service on SageMaker. GPU utilisation is only 40% during peak and requests queue during traffic bursts. Which techniques address both issues? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Enable continuous batching so multiple requests share a single forward pass
Apply quantisation (e.g., INT8) to reduce GPU memory footprint and allow more concurrent requests
Increase the Lambda timeout for the front-end service
Add more CPU instances to the SageMaker endpoint
Store model outputs in DynamoDB for reuse

explanation: Skill 2.2.2 covers token processing capacity planning and GPU utilisation. Continuous batching (also called iteration-level batching) lets the GPU process multiple in-flight requests simultaneously, improving GPU utilisation from 40% toward 80%+. INT8 quantisation halves GPU memory per model instance, enabling more concurrent batches or larger batch sizes. Lambda timeout is front-end infrastructure — doesn't affect GPU utilisation. CPU instances don't help for GPU-bound LLM inference. DynamoDB caching helps repeat queries but not novel ones.
source_topic: LLM inference optimisation, batching, quantisation, SageMaker

topic: SageMaker Async Inference for large payloads
question_text: A developer deploys a text-to-image model on SageMaker. User requests include payloads up to 35 MB (high-resolution images) and processing can take up to 8 minutes. The system must handle on-demand requests without users waiting synchronously. Which SageMaker inference type is correct?

options.text: SageMaker Real-Time Inference on a GPU instance
SageMaker Serverless Inference
SageMaker Asynchronous Inference on a GPU (accelerated computing) instance
SageMaker Batch Transform job triggered per request

explanation: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference (Skill 2.2.2 — LLM deployment strategies) supports large payloads (up to ~1 GB), long processing times (minutes), and on-demand request queuing — exactly matching 35 MB payload + 8 minute processing. Real-Time Inference caps at ~6 MB payload and ~60 second timeout — both exceeded here. Serverless Inference is convenient but does not support GPU instances, making it infeasible for image generation. Batch Transform processes offline batches — not designed for interactive on-demand requests.
source_topic: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference, inference type selection

topic: Tensor parallelism and GPU replica efficiency
question_text: A fine-tuned LLM is deployed on a SageMaker endpoint with an 8-GPU instance. Production logs show that the model's weights and activations fit within 4 GPUs, and per-instance concurrency is only 25% of capacity. Which configuration improvement maximises throughput on existing hardware?

options.text: Set tensor parallelism degree = 8 to utilise all GPUs for one model copy
Add more SageMaker instances to distribute load
Set tensor parallelism degree = 4 so the instance runs two model replicas simultaneously
Enable speculative decoding to reduce per-request latency

explanation: Skill 2.2.2 covers GPU utilisation and token processing capacity. If the model fits in 4 GPUs and the instance has 8, setting tensor parallelism = 4 allows two replicas (4 × 2 = 8 GPUs fully utilised) — doubling throughput on the same hardware. TP = 8 forces one replica across all 8 GPUs; the remaining 4 GPUs sit idle as the model doesn't need them — no throughput gain. Adding instances increases cost without fixing the per-instance utilisation waste. Speculative decoding reduces token latency but consumes extra VRAM for a draft model and does not increase concurrent replica count.
source_topic: Tensor parallelism, GPU utilisation, SageMaker

topic: Staged fine-tuned model deployment with Provisioned Throughput
question_text: A team has fine-tuned a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock and wants to deploy it for inference in a way that limits blast radius before full rollout. Which is the CORRECT deployment path for a Bedrock custom (fine-tuned) model?

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the custom model, validate it in a staging environment, then increase capacity for production after quality checks pass
Use the custom model with on-demand API calls exactly like a base model — no additional step is needed
Deploy the custom model to an EC2 instance and invoke it over SSH
Publish the custom model weights to a public S3 bucket for inference

explanation: Custom (fine-tuned) models on Amazon Bedrock require Provisioned Throughput to be purchased before they can be invoked for inference — they cannot be called on-demand like base models. The staged approach (staging PT → quality validation → production PT) limits blast radius. EC2 + SSH and a public S3 bucket are not valid Bedrock deployment paths and expose model weights unnecessarily.
source_topic: Bedrock custom model deployment, Provisioned Throughput for fine-tuned models

question_text: A team wants to quickly deploy an open-source LLM (such as Llama 3) on AWS infrastructure with a managed endpoint, without building training infrastructure from scratch. Which SageMaker feature provides a curated catalog of pre-trained models that can be deployed in one click?

options.text: SageMaker JumpStart — a model hub with pre-trained FMs and ML models deployable to SageMaker endpoints
SageMaker Ground Truth — a data labeling service
SageMaker Clarify — a model explainability tool
SageMaker Pipelines — a CI/CD workflow service for ML

explanation: SageMaker JumpStart is a model hub offering pre-trained FMs (including Llama, Mistral, and others), algorithms, and ML solutions that can be deployed to a SageMaker endpoint with minimal configuration. Ground Truth labels data, Clarify explains predictions, and Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows — none provide a model catalog for one-click deployment.
source_topic: SageMaker JumpStart, model hub, open-source LLM deployment

question_text: A company experiences highly variable Bedrock API traffic — quiet overnight, with large spikes at 9 AM and 2 PM. They receive ThrottlingException errors during peak periods. What is the MOST cost-effective fix?

options.text: Switch to on-demand pricing with no changes
Purchase Bedrock Provisioned Throughput to guarantee capacity during peak hours
Deploy a dedicated SageMaker endpoint with auto-scaling
Implement exponential backoff retries and accept the throttling

explanation: When ThrottlingExceptions occur during predictable peaks, Bedrock Provisioned Throughput is the right solution — it reserves dedicated model units that guarantee throughput during the known peak windows. Per the vicsz study notes: 'Throttling exceptions → Provisioned Capacity'. On-demand pricing alone doesn't prevent throttling. SageMaker adds unnecessary infrastructure complexity. Exponential backoff handles transient errors but doesn't solve sustained capacity shortfalls.
source_topic: Provisioned Throughput to resolve ThrottlingException

topic: DJL for high-throughput LLM inference on SageMaker
question_text: A team is hosting a 70B-parameter LLM on Amazon SageMaker using DJL (Deep Java Library) serving. GPU utilisation is low (< 40%) because prompts are much shorter than the configured max sequence length. What is the MOST targeted optimisation?

options.text: Add more GPU instances to the endpoint
Enable tensor parallelism across more GPUs
Lower the max sequence length to better match actual prompt lengths
Switch to a different embedding model

explanation: DJL's memory allocation is based on max sequence length. If prompts are much shorter than configured, GPU memory is over-provisioned per slot, leaving fewer concurrent slots (low utilisation). Reducing max sequence length to match actual usage frees memory, allows more concurrent requests per GPU, and improves utilisation — the targeted fix per the DJL tuning rule: 'Prompts much shorter than max → lower max sequence length'. Adding instances increases cost. More tensor parallelism increases inter-GPU communication overhead. Embedding models are irrelevant here.
source_topic: DJL max sequence length tuning for GPU utilisation

topic: DJL for high-throughput LLM inference on SageMaker
question_text: A team runs a 13B-parameter model on 4 GPUs via DJL tensor parallelism. GPU utilisation is low and the model fits comfortably on 2 GPUs. What is the MOST effective optimisation to improve throughput without adding instances?

options.text: Increase tensor parallelism from 4 GPUs to 8 GPUs
Reduce tensor parallelism to 2 GPUs and increase the number of model replicas on the freed GPUs
Enable prompt caching to reduce inference calls
Switch to a quantised INT4 version of the model

explanation: Per the DJL tuning rule: 'Model fits on fewer GPUs → reduce tensor parallelism, increase replicas'. Using fewer GPUs per replica (2 instead of 4) means you can run 2 replicas on the same 4 GPUs, doubling throughput. Tensor parallelism adds inter-GPU communication overhead — using the minimum needed is optimal. Increasing tensor parallelism further would worsen the overhead. Prompt caching reduces calls but doesn't improve throughput capacity. Quantisation helps latency/memory but is a separate concern.
source_topic: DJL tensor parallelism vs replicas for throughput

question_text: A company is choosing between on-demand and Provisioned Throughput for Amazon Bedrock. Their workload is unpredictable — some days very low, some days very high, with no consistent pattern. Which pricing model is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput — guarantees capacity regardless of traffic
On-demand — pay only for tokens used, no committed capacity
SageMaker Batch Transform — lowest unit cost
SageMaker Serverless Inference — scales to zero automatically

explanation: For unpredictable, spiky, or inconsistent workloads, on-demand pricing is more cost-effective because you pay only for actual usage with no hourly commitment. Provisioned Throughput bills by the hour regardless of utilisation — cost-effective only for steady, predictable workloads. Batch Transform is for large async jobs. SageMaker Serverless is for custom model inference, not Bedrock.
source_topic: On-demand Bedrock for unpredictable traffic patterns

topic: Staged fine-tuned model deployment with Provisioned Throughput
question_text: A company fine-tuned a Claude model via Amazon Bedrock. During testing, they try to invoke the fine-tuned model using on-demand pricing and receive a 'ModelNotReadyException'. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The fine-tuning job is still running
Custom (fine-tuned) models on Bedrock require Provisioned Throughput to be purchased before they can be invoked
Claude models cannot be fine-tuned on Bedrock
The IAM role lacks bedrock:InvokeModel permission

explanation: On Amazon Bedrock, custom (fine-tuned) models CANNOT be invoked using on-demand pricing. You must purchase Provisioned Throughput for the custom model before it can be invoked. This is a critical distinction: base/foundation models support on-demand, but customised models require provisioned capacity. A still-running job would show 'InProgress' status. IAM issues produce AccessDeniedException, not ModelNotReadyException.
source_topic: Custom models require Provisioned Throughput on Bedrock

question_text: A team wants to quickly deploy a pre-built open-source model (e.g., Llama 3) on Amazon SageMaker with a one-click deployment, without building a custom container or writing training code. Which SageMaker feature enables this?

options.text: SageMaker Data Wrangler
SageMaker JumpStart
SageMaker Pipelines
SageMaker Model Monitor

explanation: SageMaker JumpStart is a model hub providing one-click deployment of pre-built foundation and open-source models (including Llama, Mistral, Falcon, etc.) to SageMaker endpoints without custom containers or code. Data Wrangler is for data preparation. Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows. Model Monitor detects drift in deployed models.
source_topic: SageMaker JumpStart for one-click model deployment

question_text: To reduce inference costs, a team wants to try a small, cheap model first for each request, and only escalate to a large, expensive model if the small model's response confidence is below a threshold. What is this pattern called?

options.text: Circuit breaker pattern
Model cascading (tiered FM usage)
Semantic caching
Hybrid search

explanation: Model cascading (also called tiered FM usage) routes requests first to a cheap, smaller model. If the response meets quality/confidence requirements, the pipeline stops — saving cost. If not, it escalates to a more capable, expensive model. This optimises the cost-quality trade-off. Circuit breaker handles service failures. Semantic caching returns cached responses for similar queries. Hybrid search combines keyword and vector retrieval.
source_topic: Model cascading for cost-quality trade-off

question_text: A team needs to deploy a large open-source LLM on Amazon SageMaker with optimised GPU serving, continuous batching, and support for multiple concurrent requests. Which SageMaker container type is purpose-built for this?

options.text: SageMaker built-in XGBoost container
SageMaker Large Model Inference (LMI) container with DJL
SageMaker Sklearn container
AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) for PyTorch training

explanation: SageMaker Large Model Inference (LMI) containers with DJL (Deep Java Library) are purpose-built for hosting large language models with GPU-optimised serving features: continuous batching, tensor parallelism, and efficient memory management for multi-GPU inference. XGBoost and Sklearn containers are for traditional ML models. PyTorch training DLCs are for training, not inference serving.
source_topic: SageMaker LMI containers for LLM inference

question_text: A high-traffic GenAI application frequently receives semantically similar (but not identical) questions like 'What is the refund policy?' and 'How do I get a refund?'. The team wants to serve cached responses for semantically similar queries to reduce inference costs. Which caching technique achieves this?

options.text: Deterministic hash-based caching in ElastiCache (Redis)
HTTP response caching at the CloudFront edge
Semantic caching using vector embeddings to find near-identical cached responses
Lambda local memory caching of recent responses

explanation: Semantic caching embeds the incoming query, searches a vector store (MemoryDB or OpenSearch) for cached queries with high embedding similarity, and returns the cached response if the semantic distance is below a threshold. This handles paraphrases and variations. Hash-based caching only hits exact matches. CloudFront caching is for static content, not dynamic LLM responses. Lambda memory cache is per-instance and ephemeral.
source_topic: Semantic caching with vector similarity for GenAI cost reduction

topic: SageMaker Async Inference for large payloads
question_text: A document processing application submits very large documents (up to 500 pages) for summarisation. The processing takes 2-5 minutes per document and synchronous API calls time out. Which SageMaker inference mode is MOST appropriate?

options.text: SageMaker Real-Time Inference
SageMaker Serverless Inference
SageMaker Asynchronous Inference
SageMaker Batch Transform

explanation: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference is designed for large payloads and long-running processing (up to 15 minutes). It accepts the request, queues it, and returns the result to an S3 bucket asynchronously — no timeout issues. Real-Time Inference has a 60-second response timeout. Serverless Inference also times out for long requests. Batch Transform is for very large batch jobs with minimal latency requirements, not on-demand per-document requests.
source_topic: SageMaker Async Inference for large, long-running payloads

question_text: A team has purchased Bedrock Provisioned Throughput and monitors ModelInvocationUtilization in CloudWatch. The utilisation is consistently at 15%. What does this indicate and what should they do?

options.text: The model is healthy; no action needed
They are over-provisioned and wasting money; they should reduce provisioned model units or switch to on-demand
They need more provisioned units to increase capacity
Utilisation below 20% triggers automatic scaling of provisioned units

explanation: Bedrock Provisioned Throughput bills by the hour regardless of utilisation. 15% utilisation means 85% of purchased capacity is idle and being paid for unnecessarily. The team should reduce model units to better match actual demand, or switch to on-demand pricing. Optimal utilisation for cost-efficiency is typically 70-90%. There is no automatic scaling of provisioned units.
source_topic: Provisioned Throughput utilisation monitoring and right-sizing

topic: Bedrock Cross-Region Inference for performance routing
question_text: A global application serves users in North America, Europe, and Asia. The team wants to route each inference request to the geographically nearest AWS region to minimise latency, while keeping the same model. Which Bedrock feature achieves this?

options.text: Bedrock Cross-Region Inference for failover
Bedrock Inference Profiles for multi-region performance routing
Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing
Amazon CloudFront with Lambda@Edge

explanation: Bedrock Inference Profiles enable multi-region performance routing — routing requests to the optimal region for lowest latency, not just failover. Cross-Region Inference is for availability/failover when one region is unavailable. Route 53 and CloudFront/Lambda@Edge are general-purpose networking tools that don't manage Bedrock model routing natively.
source_topic: Bedrock Inference Profiles for multi-region latency routing
